claims.text: A high-entropy alloy contains at least five elements, each at no less than 5 atomic percent.
The proposed baseline is a single-phase solid solution with a balanced mixture of lighter and heavier transition metals.
In single-phase HEAs, superconducting transition temperature is governed by electron–phonon coupling.
The electron–phonon coupling in these HEAs is modulated by the fraction of heavy transition metals.
Increasing the heavy-transition-metal fraction enhances lattice distortion.
Increasing the heavy-transition-metal fraction alters the phonon density of states.
The resulting lattice distortion and phonon-spectrum shift strengthen electron–phonon coupling.
Changes in electron–phonon coupling modify Cooper pairing and therefore the superconducting transition temperature.
The heavy-transition-metal fraction will be increased incrementally while synthesis, processing, and the high-entropy constraint are held constant.
Samples with higher heavy-transition-metal content should show a systematic change in superconducting transition temperature relative to the baseline.
Higher heavy-transition-metal content is likely to increase transition temperature or alter the upper critical field.
Changes in superconducting properties should correlate with measured changes in lattice vibrational properties.
The proposed heavy-element relationship is expected to apply only while the alloy remains a single-phase solid solution.
Phase separation or secondary-phase precipitation can invalidate a simple relationship between heavy-element content and superconductivity.
Disorder, multielement interactions, and nonlinear phonon contributions may compensate for the proposed heavy-element effect and make the magnitude of transition-temperature modulation uncertain.
A lack of systematic change in transition temperature or associated phonon behavior as heavy-element content increases would falsify the proposed mechanism.
